name: Monthly Department Performance Update
description: For department heads and monthly leadership syncs: navy-and-warm-white structure, amber cadence markers, compact goal and project ledgers, quantified team output, explicit resource asks, and owner-based next-month commitments.
style_guide:
# Monthly Department Performance Update

## Design intent

Create a concise monthly operating update for one department, function, or delivery team. The deck should turn one reporting month into a clear management story: overall score, goals, active projects, team output, blockers and resource decisions, then next-month commitments. It is practical, candid, and easy to scan in a leadership sync. Deep navy supplies authority, warm white keeps dense evidence readable, amber marks cadence and management attention, green records verified progress, and red isolates a real miss or blocker.

This is a recurring monthly control document, not a quarterly strategy review, annual retrospective, or generic dashboard. Keep the time horizon short, comparisons consistent, owners visible, and decisions concrete. Every page should communicate one operational conclusion and show what changed since the prior month. Preserve the visual grammar shown by the previews, but never copy their company, people, department, projects, metrics, dates, vendors, resource requests, or commitments. Preview images are UI-only references; this written guide is the complete authoring authority.

## Core visual signature

- Use a split navy-and-warm-white cover followed by predominantly warm-white analytical pages.
- Pair very large, heavy sans-serif headlines with small tracked monospaced metadata for periods, units, page codes, statuses, and due dates.
- Use Amber as the cadence and management-attention accent: reporting periods, section rules, active timeline nodes, callout labels, and decision prompts.
- Reserve Green for verified achievement or favorable movement and Red for a material miss, high-severity issue, or breached threshold.
- Use Deep navy for structure, score cards, collaboration panels, decision bars, and the strongest total or target.
- Build pages from aligned rows, ledgers, progress bars, KPI cards, and owner-based commitments. Avoid decorative illustration and dashboard ornament.
- End each body page with one short operational takeaway, watchpoint, signal, ask, or next-review note at bottom-left and a quiet `NN / NN` counter at bottom-right.

## Canvas, grid, and spacing

- Use a fixed `1280 × 720 px` canvas in a 16:9 ratio.
- Keep `64–68 px` left and right safe margins and `24–34 px` top and bottom safe margins. No owner, status, due date, or source may touch the canvas edge.
- Use a 12-column grid with `16–22 px` gutters. Align title edges, KPI cards, ledger columns, progress bars, owner blocks, decision bands, and footer notes to shared grid lines.
- Body pages reserve roughly `94–118 px` for the navigation row, section label, title, and subtitle. Leave `24–34 px` before the primary exhibit.
- Use `18–24 px` between major panels and `10–16 px` within KPI cards, ledger rows, and issue modules.
- Prefer one dominant exhibit and one supporting exhibit. A page may contain several rows, but it should not contain several competing dashboards.
- Use square corners or a maximum `2–4 px` radius. Cards are flat and border-led, with no drop shadows.
- The cover uses a roughly `58/42` split: a Deep-navy narrative field on the left and a Warm-white at-a-glance field on the right.

## Color system

### Foundation colors

- Department navy: `#102E4A`. Use for the cover field, major titles, score cards, collaboration panels, decision bars, primary progress bars, and active timeline nodes.
- Warm white: `#F7F6F2`. Use as the dominant body-page canvas and the cover summary field.
- Pure white: `#FFFFFF`. Use for score cards, KPI cards, ledgers, issue cards, commitment cards, and analytical panels.
- Cool panel: `#F2F5F8`. Use for ledger headers, progress tracks, neutral grouping, and alternating evidence rows.
- Primary ink: `#0D2B47`. Use for headlines, project names, values, owners, actions, and decisive statements.
- Body slate: `#52627A`. Use for subtitles, explanations, qualifiers, chart labels, and roles.
- Quiet steel: `#8A9AAF`. Use for inactive values, prior-period context, page metadata, and subdued annotations.
- Structural line: `#DDE5EC`. Use for one-pixel borders, ledger rules, chart grids, dividers, and timeline rails.

### Cadence and status colors

- Cadence amber: `#E9A92B`. Use for reporting-period labels, section markers, active commitments, attention notes, watchpoints, decision prompts, and the current bar in a historical score trend.
- Achievement green: `#2DA06A`. Use only for achieved goals, on-track delivery, verified favorable movement, completed actions, and controlled conditions.
- Issue red: `#D34A4A`. Use only for missed goals, high-severity blockers, at-risk projects, breached thresholds, unfavorable movement, or overdue decisions.
- Pale green: `#E5F3EC`. Use behind Green status labels.
- Pale red: `#F8E7E6`. Use behind Red status labels.
- Pale amber: `#FBF1D9`. Use sparingly behind an Amber watch label or attention note.

### Color discipline

- Department navy carries hierarchy and structure; it is not a performance status.
- Amber identifies cadence, attention, and the active reporting moment. It does not automatically mean risk.
- Green and Red require explicit rules. Publish the relevant target, threshold, comparison, or decision state beside the color.
- Do not introduce a generic yellow RAG state unless the department has a defined watch threshold. If Amber means watch on a page, label it `WATCH` and state the rule.
- Keep saturated fills small: narrow top rails, compact badges, bars, dots, values, or one dark panel. Ordinary body pages remain predominantly Warm white and Pure white.
- Never rely on color alone. Pair every status with direct words such as `ACHIEVED`, `ON TRACK`, `AT RISK`, `MISSED`, `HIGH SEVERITY`, or a localized equivalent.
- Use flat fills only. Avoid gradients, glow, glass effects, colored shadows, and decorative textures.

## Typography

- Primary font: `Inter`, with `Arial`, `Helvetica Neue`, or a comparable system sans-serif as fallback.
- Metadata font: `IBM Plex Mono`, with `Consolas` or `Courier New` as fallback. Use it for slide codes, reporting periods, dates, units, status notes, progress annotations, sources, and page counters.
- For CJK output, use a common CJK sans-serif with strong bold weights and a CJK-capable monospaced face only for short metadata. Preserve hierarchy without forcing Latin tracking conventions.
- Cover title: `58–68 px`, weight `800–900`, line-height `1.0–1.06`, Pure white. Use two or three deliberate lines.
- Cover eyebrow and reporting period: `11–14 px`, metadata face, weight `600–700`, uppercase when appropriate, letter-spacing `2.5–4 px`, Pure white or Cadence amber.
- Body-page title: `36–44 px`, weight `800–900`, line-height `1.02–1.1`, Primary ink. Write it as the operating subject or conclusion.
- Subtitle: `15–18 px`, weight `400–500`, line-height `1.4–1.5`, Body slate. State the monthly result, variance, or management context.
- Hero score: `48–66 px`, weight `800–900`, tabular numerals. KPI value: `34–48 px`, weight `800–900`.
- Project, issue, or commitment title: `17–22 px`, weight `700–800`, line-height `1.12–1.25`.
- Body copy and ledger details: `11–14 px`, weight `400–600`, line-height `1.35–1.55`.
- Owners, targets, statuses, and important qualifiers: `11–14 px`, weight `600–800`.
- Navigation, section labels, table headers, units, dates, sources, progress notes, and footer labels: `8–10 px`, metadata face, weight `600–700`, letter-spacing `1.2–2.2 px`.
- Do not shrink text to fit another KPI, project, issue, or commitment. Summarize or move detail to backup pages.

## Page frame and navigation

- Begin each body page with a small Amber vertical marker followed by the department or function name and `MONTHLY REVIEW` at upper-left. Put the reporting period or planning month at upper-right.
- Separate the navigation row from content with a one-pixel Structural line.
- Place a small Amber monospaced section label such as `02 — GOALS` above the title.
- Use one strong left-aligned title and one sentence summarizing the result or management context.
- A score, total ask, or target-month score may appear in one Deep-navy card at upper-right. It must not displace the title or become a decorative duplicate.
- Keep the lower rule quiet. Use the bottom-left note for a specific takeaway, watchpoint, signal, ask, or next-review date.
- The page counter uses compact monospaced text at bottom-right and remains outside the main evidence panels.

## Cover and at-a-glance scorecard

- Use the `58/42` navy-and-warm-white split. The left field contains department identity, reporting period, title, one-sentence purpose, presenter, department, review date, and document classification.
- Use a faint, oversized grid on the navy field and no more than two thin decorative circles: one Amber crop near the split and one outlined circle near the lower boundary. Decoration stays behind content.
- The right field starts with a compact `AT-A-GLANCE` label and a short statement such as the number of KPIs, one department, and one story.
- Show one dominant Overall Month Score card with score basis, target, and prior-month variance. Never show a composite score without defining how it is calculated.
- Add no more than three supporting KPI cards beneath the score. Each contains one label, value, and one short status or comparison.
- Finish with a compact five- or six-period bar trend. Highlight only the current month in Amber and label every period consistently.
- Do not reuse the preview's score, department, date, presenter, KPI count, or trend values.

## Goals and completion status

- Show three to six monthly goals in a full-width ledger. Use columns for goal, target, actual, progress, and status.
- The goal label includes a short definition or population so the metric is auditable.
- Use a thin progress track and a Green, Navy, Amber, or Red fill according to the defined status. Put a monospaced variance or completion note directly beneath the bar.
- Use compact rectangular status labels. `ACHIEVED` means the published target was met; `MISSED` means it was not. If partial, deferred, or watch states exist, define them explicitly.
- A composite goal score may sit in a Deep-navy card at upper-right. State weighting, goal count, scale, and target.
- The bottom takeaway identifies the single most material miss, its impact, and where the remediation or decision appears.
- For inverse metrics such as response time, backlog, errors, or cost, make the desired direction explicit. Do not calculate progress as though higher is always better.

## Core projects and delivery ledger

- Start with three compact status-count cards at upper-right: on track, ahead, and at risk, or the department's equivalent states. Counts must reconcile to the visible project set or be labeled as a subset.
- Use a ledger with columns for sequence, project, owner, progress, key metric, and status.
- Each project row contains one concise project name, one scope line, one accountable owner, one progress bar, one dated progress note or next gate, one outcome metric, and one explicit status.
- Keep progress and outcome separate. A project can be 100 percent delivered without producing the intended outcome; label both honestly.
- Use Green for on track, Navy for ahead or complete when a separate positive state is needed, and Red for at risk. Do not use Green for an ahead state if Green already means on plan.
- Show no more than five or six primary projects on a main slide. Move portfolio detail to an appendix rather than shrinking rows.
- End with one watchpoint naming the project, dependency, decision owner, and date that threatens the next milestone.

## Team output and collaboration

- Use a row of four KPI cards for volume, speed, quality, and collaboration or another balanced set relevant to the function.
- Each card contains a label, hero value, prior-month variance, and one driver or sample note. Use an arrow only when the desired direction is clear.
- Below the KPI row, use a `6/6` split. The left side shows one ranked output chart by pod, team, region, or workstream; the right side uses a Deep-navy collaboration panel.
- Output bars use Department navy by default. Use one Amber bar to highlight the selected or constrained group, not simply the largest value.
- State headcount or denominator beside each group so raw volume is not mistaken for productivity.
- Collaboration highlights use numbered Amber indices and three concise rows. Each row states the cross-functional action, participating teams, quantified result, and date or cadence.
- Do not equate higher output with better performance without quality, workload, capacity, or customer context.

## Issues, resource needs, and decisions

- Use one Total Ask card at upper-right when the issues require budget, headcount, tooling, vendor, or leadership decisions. State the components and avoid double counting.
- Present no more than three primary issue cards in equal columns. Use a Red top rail for high severity and Amber for medium or watch severity.
- Each issue card contains: severity, concise issue statement, causal context, quantified impact, one accountable owner, the exact ask, cost or capacity implication, expected outcome, and a decision-needed-by date.
- Use a Deep-navy decision bar at the bottom of each card. The date is a real decision deadline, not a decorative milestone.
- Distinguish incident remediation, temporary capacity, permanent headcount, software licenses, vendor work, and policy decisions. Do not combine unlike requests into a vague resource need.
- State the basis for payback, cost avoidance, service recovery, or schedule protection. Label estimates and assumptions explicitly.
- The bottom Ask note explains which forum owns the decisions and what target slips if approval is deferred.

## Next-month plan and owners

- Use a horizontal weekly timeline with four weekly nodes plus an end-of-month node when the calendar fits. Adapt the number of nodes to the actual month and reporting cadence.
- Place one commitment card below each node. Every card contains a commitment number, action-led title, one accountable owner, measurable target or definition of done, and due date.
- Use Amber for the first and final milestone or another meaningful active anchor; ordinary intermediate nodes use Department navy. Do not alternate colors decoratively.
- Keep five commitments or fewer on a main page. Multiple contributors may be listed, but one directly responsible owner must remain clear.
- A target-month score card may sit at upper-right only if the scoring method is stable and the target links to the commitments.
- End with the exact next-review date, time, cadence, or reporting expectation.
- Commitments must follow from the current month's goals, projects, issues, and decisions. Avoid adding unrelated aspirational work.

## Charts, progress bars, and score logic

- Prefer six-period bar trends, compact horizontal progress bars, ranked bars, target-versus-actual rows, status counts, owner-based ledgers, and weekly commitment timelines.
- Use Department navy for the primary series, Amber for the current reporting month or active focus, Green for verified favorable status, Red for a breach or risk, and Quiet steel for history or inactive states.
- Use Structural line for grids and tracks. Keep axes simple and directly label important values.
- Every metric requires a unit, reporting period, scope, source or system, and comparator or target where applicable.
- Show the score formula, weighting, normalization, target, and treatment of missing data before presenting a composite month or goal score.
- Do not crop axes to exaggerate movement. When only six monthly values exist, label all six rather than implying a continuous long-term trend.
- Distinguish completed work, delivered output, realized outcome, current run rate, forecast, and next-month target.
- For percentage-point changes, use `pts` or `pp`; do not label them as percent growth.

## Adaptable composition families

These are composition tendencies, not executable templates, a mandatory sequence, or permission to reuse preview content. Choose the structure that best supports the department's actual monthly story.

- Cover and monthly scorecard: use the navy/warm-white split with reporting metadata, one composite score, three supporting KPIs, and a short historical trend.
- Goals: use a goal ledger with target, actual, progress annotation, status, and one score card.
- Project portfolio: use status-count cards above a five- or six-row owner-based project ledger.
- Team performance: use four KPI cards above a ranked output exhibit and one collaboration or capability panel.
- Issues and asks: use a total-ask summary and up to three severity-coded issue cards with impact, owner, ask, cost, and decision deadline.
- Next-month plan: use a weekly timeline with up to five commitment cards, named owners, targets, due dates, and the next-review cadence.
- Service department alternative: use demand volume, response time, quality, backlog, staffing, and escalation metrics with channel or pod breakdowns.
- Sales department alternative: use bookings, pipeline, conversion, cycle time, forecast accuracy, key deals, enablement blockers, and next-month commitments.
- Marketing department alternative: use sourced pipeline, campaign delivery, channel efficiency, content production, experiments, dependencies, and next-month launch dates.
- Product or engineering alternative: use roadmap delivery, reliability, adoption, quality, cycle time, technical blockers, staffing asks, and dated release commitments.
- Finance or people alternative: adapt the metrics and terminology while retaining exact definitions, owners, due dates, and the monthly accountability rhythm.

## Content truth and monthly reporting controls

- Treat every preview organization, person, metric, project, department, vendor, score, target, date, cost, and request as fictional reference content. Never reuse it unless independently grounded in the current Workspace.
- Never invent KPI values, project progress, quality scores, customer metrics, productivity, headcount, cost, savings, payback, targets, incidents, vendors, deadlines, or resource requests.
- State the exact reporting month, data-lock timestamp, timezone where material, population, currency, and departmental scope.
- Use the same definition and comparison base month to month. If a metric definition changed, disclose the break and do not present the series as continuous.
- Distinguish target, stretch target, forecast, actual, preliminary actual, plan, and management estimate.
- Status rules must be published and stable. Improvement alone does not mean on track; deterioration alone does not mean missed if the target remains met.
- Project percent complete must have a defined basis. Avoid false precision when progress is a qualitative estimate.
- For team output, include capacity, headcount, working days, case mix, or another relevant denominator before making productivity claims.
- For resource asks, state requested quantity, one-time and recurring cost, timing, decision owner, expected effect, assumptions, and consequence of delay.
- Each action or commitment needs one accountable owner, measurable definition of done, due date, dependency where material, and review cadence.
- If evidence is incomplete, label it preliminary, show the data gap, use a clearly marked `TBD`, or omit the claim. Never fill a monthly report with plausible numbers.

## Allowed variation

- Preserve the navy/warm-white split cover, predominantly light body pages, Amber cadence markers, exact Green/Red semantics, heavy sans-serif headlines, monospaced metadata, square cards, owner discipline, and visible dates.
- The update may cover a department, function, region, delivery team, shared service, or program. Adapt KPI names and operating language without changing the accountability grammar.
- Use three to five goals, three to six projects, three or four team KPIs, up to three primary issues, and up to five next-month commitments according to the available evidence.
- A body page may use one Deep-navy panel or score card. Do not turn every page dark.
- Adapt capitalization, tracking, line breaks, number formats, date formats, and status words to the confirmed output language while keeping thresholds explicit.
- If the department has a stable brand accent, it may replace Amber only when it remains clearly distinct from Green and Red status colors.

## Avoid

- Do not reproduce preview facts, people, projects, dates, resource asks, vendors, or metrics. Transfer the monthly operating grammar only.
- Do not turn the deck into a quarterly strategy review, annual narrative, board pre-read, or generic KPI dashboard. Keep the one-month change and next-month ownership visible.
- Do not use gradients, photography, decorative illustration, 3D charts, glass effects, glow, rounded SaaS cards, floating icons, or ornamental blobs.
- Do not use Green, Amber, or Red as arbitrary department colors. Preserve their stated meaning.
- Do not show a composite score without formula, weights, scale, target, and missing-data treatment.
- Do not report project completion without an outcome or next gate, and do not report team output without quality or capacity context.
- Do not list blockers without severity, impact, owner, exact ask, cost or capacity implication, and decision deadline.
- Do not use commitments without measurable targets, owners, and dates.
- Do not show more than six goals, six projects, four ordinary KPI cards, three primary issues, or five commitments on one main slide. Move detail to an appendix.
- Do not shrink sources, progress notes, owner names, statuses, or deadlines below readable size.
- Do not hide misses, change thresholds after the period closes, mix reporting windows, or compare unlike populations.
